en: Re-31344 ॥ Commentary on the Yatidharmabodhini ॥
The symbols *u* (ū),
*śrīsundaragaṇapataye namaḥ*,
and *dots* (... are used to indicate missing portions, leaf damage, or unidentified characters.
Words or letters within brackets are my suggestions (based on my understanding).
Red coloring indicates (possible) errors, primarily occurring at the seventh line from each side.
The Explanation of the *Yatidharmabodhini* (The Enlightenment of the Duties of Ascetics)
Om. Salutations to Śrī Sundaragaṇapati;
salutations to Śrī Mahāgaṇapati.
May there be auspiciousness in this *Yatidharmaprabodhinī*.
I worship Viśveśa, Janmāyavana, Dhundhi, Daṇḍapāṇi, and Bhairava; I worship Kāśī, Guhā, Gaṅgā, Bhavānī, and Maṇikarṇikā.

Having heard the words of the preceptor of preceptors, the foremost essence of the beloved of Śrī, whose compassion is manifested through speech, I bow to the Guru who is the half of Śrī Śaṅkara, the destroyer of the sins of the Kali age descended upon the earth, the soul of all. And thus, requested by the venerable Sage Nārada—who was unable to bear the previous burden—Parameśvara himself, having been entreated by the Grandfather (Brahmā), has fortunately appeared on earth in human form as the one named Śrī Śaṅkarabhāratī, as a portion of his own self.

The intention is heard [in the scriptures] that, having understood that the salutation to one’s great preceptor (*mahāguru*) alone is the salutation to all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), based on the authoritative statement of the learned, "O Vata-tāra! Indeed, it is stated in the *Yogaśikhā Upaniṣad*: "The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the god Sadāśiva; there is nothing whatsoever superior to the Guru. And: "One should worship with supreme devotion the Preceptor, the Supreme Lord, who is the teacher of the knowledge of liberation.

"...one shall obtain the fruit of knowledge. Thus he describes his own salutation to the Guru: "I, Nīlakaṇṭha Yati, who resides in the divine abode on the bank of the [river] in the midst of the city of Śrī-Kāśikā, and who is a servant at the feet of the venerable Śiva-Śaṅkarendra Miśra, the ocean of compassion, bow to my own soul with full devotion."

Salutations to the supreme ones; salutations to the supreme sages. Here, indeed, in this city of Śrī-Kāśī, which is renowned as a land of merit (*puṇyabhūmi*) and serves as a great ornament to the earth, there were those who had descended [to this world] through a lineage of many various families. Among them, by the son of the venerable Sudhākara Sūri—whose secondary name was Bhāṇḍa—and who belonged to the Kauṇḍinya *gotra*... [the work was composed]. [Note: The text fragment provided appears to be an opening portion of an inscription or colophon, likely from a Sanskrit manuscript. It identifies the author’s lineage, his spiritual preceptor (*ātma-guru*), and the location of composition.]

In this *Śrībhāgavata-vyākhyā-ratnamālā*, composed by Nīlakaṇṭha Vipaścit, consisting of three thousand and fifty verses, titled *Traivaṇika-dharmaprakāśikā*— by him who has entered the state of a Paramahaṃsa through the power of knowledge and dispassion,

and by the command of the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarayati-Indra— this treatise is now being composed, which brings forth the dharma that is gentle, long, and beautiful with words that reach the heart of the Upanishads. In it, the Vedic path of conduct, endowed with the Brahman, is set forth together with its roots, for the easy understanding of those seeking liberation.

In this [work], while investigating the basis [of authority], the path of Vedic revelation and traditional practice has been established by means of its supporting texts—the *Skanda Purāṇa* and others, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* composed by Parāśara, and the *Kalpasūtras* of Baudhāyana and others. Thus, the stainlessness of the Veda is clearly manifested. As for the *Kalpasūtras*, because they are authoritative for those who know the cities [the sacred sites] and the lineages (*gotras*), their status as valid means of knowledge is certain; should anyone here harbor doubt regarding this—

When even the Brahminhood of one who has fallen away from that conduct is called into question, how much more so for those who have authored great Purāṇas that contradict the entire Veda? For the authority of works such as the *Kādambarī*, which were composed independently [of the Vedas], cannot be established due to their lack of a root; rather, it is said that they must be cultivated only when they possess a root. Furthermore, because they are easy to understand and pleasant for those seeking peace to comprehend, it is heard elsewhere that even though they are adorned with poetic figures, they are merely another form of ignorance. Indeed, it is stated in the *Parivrājaka-śruti*: "One should not become attached to weapons, nor should one live by them as a means of livelihood; one should abandon excessive speech. (I.5a, l.1)

I shall not rely upon any other position... In the *Brahmagītās*, it is said that worldly sciences directly cause the cycle of transmigration for those who possess debts [to them], whereas the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) brings about the destruction of the darkness of saṃsāra and dispels the two-fold evil of its consequences.

He who contemplates the Great Lord for the sake of the supreme goal of man, and who manifests the linga of renunciation as vast as the great ocean—he is Puruṣottama. He who, having investigated how even a mere fragment of happiness within the pursuit of dharma and other goals is ultimately preceded by suffering, seeks liberation alone; he, Maitreya, [is the one]. For the deluded, though endowed with the conduct of the six castes and stages of life, obtain fruits in accordance with their actions. But those who completely abandon the duties of caste and so forth, being satisfied in their own bliss, become true *puruṣas*.

The Great Person, having resorted to the supportless, remains established in that very state of *samaya*. Therefore, for one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), [that state] is to be attained. Even beyond that, because it is the supreme means of transition, Mahādeva is the highest, being the foremost among those who have transcended time. Through the supreme yoga, the realization of his own perfectly partless form arises for him who bears the form of Śambhu, and not by any other cause. Therefore, they say that through the attainment of the state of the Great Renunciation (*pāramahaṃsya*), which is the mark of great dispassion, or even through austerity, the fruit [is realized], as stated in the *Āditya-phaṇā*.

Even though that previously mentioned state of seeking liberation (*umukṣutva*) and the triad of *śiva-jyātra* exist, direct liberation is not accomplished in the absence of the mark of dispassion (*vairāgyaliṅga*). Now, he introduces the subject at hand: "Formerly, indeed, the characteristics of a mendicant (*bhikṣu*) and so forth were taught by Śiva alone to a yogi who was an emanation of the Three-eyed One (*triṇetra*) and had arisen from yoga. Devoted to my guru, I shall now speak of that in brief, O wise ones, as the essence of all scriptures, which bestows great bliss upon those with good ears."

Formerly, the root-guru Śiva [bestowed] upon Dūṣāsa the characteristics of a mendicant and so forth, ending with the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*); furthermore, the lord of sages performed the rite of Śaiva renunciation (*śaivasannyāsavidhi*). Then the son of Atri, Dūṣāsa, instructed his disciple; beginning with these words, I shall today speak that very same [teaching], which is for the sake of the purification of the auspicious, heard through the ears, and bestowing happiness upon the mind.

(1.5) Now, if it is argued that since there are many [traditions] such as the *Jaḍabharata* and others, how can this [work]—which has curses and weapons as its weapons—be considered an expansion of instruction? If it is said that other [works] are not so, then [we reply]: no, because elsewhere there are signs such as the introduction of this kind [of teaching]. Furthermore: "The student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣuka*)—these are the four stages of life (*āśrama*), each characterized by distinct conduct. (1.7) These four were the founders of the stages of life for the sages, namely Dadhīci, Gautama, Aṅgiras, and Durvāsas, respectively.

Having extracted the mantra from the hermitage... "O Hara," according to the word of Śiva, because he is the founder of that hermitage, its authority is established solely by what was taught by him. Furthermore, since [the world] is held fast by the weapon of his curse... it is likewise appropriate that Parameśvara, through this very [mantra], is the cause of the arising of Brahman, as is stated in various ways.

Therefore, by one who follows [this path], through the procedure for the division of time, the very characteristics such as the entry into the state of a wandering ascetic (*sannyāsa*), the conduct of a practitioner, and the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are established as the means for attaining liberation. Because it is declared in the *Sannyāsa* [Upaniṣads] and so forth, it is called "Vedic" (*vaidika*). Furthermore, because its root is the hundred-fold Vedānta, it is also called "Vedic-auditory" (*vaidika-śrauta*). This dharma of the Paramahaṃsa, being propounded by the Vedānta and taught by Śiva, is the Vedic-auditory procedure for renunciation (*vaidika-sannyāsa-vidhi*). It is [also] the Śaiva-auditory...

The meaning is that it is called "great" (*mahat*). For this very reason, it is stated that those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) should enter upon the stages of life (*āśrama*), beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*). Now, one might object: "But the Śruti says, 'One should live a hundred years performing action,' and there are Janaka and others who attained perfection through action; thus, since liberation is obtained even through the householder's stage (*gārhasthya*), how can the abandonment of action by one who has entered the [higher] stages be the cause of liberation? If this is asked, the answer is: By the force of the word "should desire to live" (*jijīviṣet*), the injunction for performance refers only to the identification with the body (*dehābhimāna*). It does not apply to one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), as that would lead to contradiction.

...the world of the pure—thus it is established by such censuring statements. However, the examples of Janaka and others taught by the Blessed One should be understood as being for the purpose of the present method of exposition. Otherwise, if one were to say, "I speak thus because the practice of celibacy is difficult to maintain," there would be no occasion for such a statement. Therefore, renunciation alone is the giver of happiness, as stated in passages such as, "Those who are well-settled through the realization of Vedānta... and "The yoga of renunciation."

"When the desires that dwell in one's heart are released from all sides, then one becomes immortal" (KaU 2.3.14). For them, austerity, celibacy, and truth are the means; for them, that stainless world of Brahman is attained. Regarding the passage beginning with "Having renounced this world... and "O, I am departing from this state," the Śruti declares that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) alone is one's duty as the supreme means. As it is said: "Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a Brāhmaṇa should take to renunciation. (MuU 1.2.12)

Liberation cannot occur through action performed in a gradual sequence. Having thoroughly examined and reflected upon the world fashioned by karma—such as the [heavenly] realms and so forth—one should become dispassionate. In the *Yogopaniṣad* it is said: "Calamities come for a moment, and prosperities come for a moment; birth and death last for a moment, like one standing on the edge of a snake's fang. Having drunk from the well dug by former [beings], one is born again in that very same place from which one was previously born. Thus is this wheel of saṃsāra.

[He] performed the *dhaṭājapa* according to the *Mahopaniṣad*. This is the time of the serpent’s withdrawal; here there is no [need for] worldly activity toward the wicked. In this [time], there is a manifestation of the devouring of mouth-to-mouth [food]. (l. 2) In the cremation grounds and at the ends of the quarters... the breasts of women are licked like a swift lump of food. Those who possess hair as dark as water and eyes that are difficult to behold are dear [to him]. (l. 3) The flame of the fire of evil deeds burns the man like a wound; even the mountains are crushed and the stars are shattered. Even the oceans dry up, and even the young... like a forest. Thus (l. 4).

Having reflected, one should indeed resort to the cessation of enmity; for liberation, which is by nature eternally established, is not produced by an action performed—it is not [produced] by what has been done. But [one might ask]: how [can this be so] in the case of the Agnihotra and other such rites, which are prescribed in the Śruti?

If it is argued that "devotion (*devana*) is the supreme good," [we reply: no, because that is not accepted as the head of the Veda (*śruti-śiraḥ*), and if it were not so accepted, impiety (*abrahmaṇya*) would be heard [in the scriptures]. In the *Vajrasūcī*, for those who pride themselves on the body being the Self, there is the crushing of the pride of the body; it is said that the one who has become a god, having been struck down, exits through the urinary passage. Furthermore, from the hearing of the great loss: "If one has known this here, then there is truth; but if one has not known this here, then a great destruction occurs. And: "They desire to know this very [Self] through the recitation of the Vedas, through sacrifice... (I.7b, l.1).

Since it is heard that "that Self is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon," and because the collection of ritual actions becomes redundant through the hearing, reflection, and understanding [of the Self], one who possesses dispassion should perform the hearing [of the scriptures] after renouncing [worldly life], according to the maxim: "One should hear [the scriptures] having renounced. Thus, following the injunctions of the Śruti, I shall now describe renunciation, as well as the lack of qualification for it and the characteristics of the various types of renouncers.

Now, after the *śūdra* [initiation], those who are immediately subsequent are: the *parivrājaka*, the eunuch (*ṣaṇḍa*), the *udhava*, the one deficient in limbs (*vikala*), the one without offspring (*aja*), the child (*bālaka*), and also the one suffering from wind-disease (*vātaruk*). Furthermore, the outcaste (*patita*), the one who has taken a boon (*varadvārī*), the *vaikhānasa*, the twice-born (*dvija*), the practitioner of the *cakrīla*, the heretic (*pāṣaṇḍī*), the *śibi*, the *viṣṭa*, and the one without a wife (*anagnika*). Also, one who has renounced the world (*saṃnyasta*) two or three times, and even the teacher of the *mṛtaka* and so forth; likewise, one who has renounced the world two or three times for the sake of the *mṛtaka* and so forth. By these, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is not permitted, except in the case of one afflicted by illness, and without following the proper sequence.

"One who is learned, whose heart is tranquil, devoted to the guru, and has conquered the senses"—such qualities as these are also stated [as requirements for eligibility]. (l. 6) ...And in that [text] it is said: "One who has reached the further shore of the six sciences, the best among the learned, superior in all his faculties, and proficient in the eternal and the non-eternal...; one who is seventy years of age, who has seen the face of a grandson, and whose teeth have fallen out; one who has emerged from the three desires—regarding renunciation, it is said... (l. 7) ...This is indeed the renunciation of the wise (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*); such is the established position of the truth. Even one afflicted by disease, always hungry, even one whose life is in danger, one who is unsatisfied, one who eats everything, or one who is a gossip about the world—(i. 8a, l. 1)

The *vicāraka* (investigator) is considered to be of middle quality if he is born of a noble lineage, possesses learning, and is self-controlled. However, one who is excessively afflicted, a child, a youth, wrathful, deceitful, prone to breaking promises and oaths, or motivated by enmity toward his father, wife, elders, wealth, grain, or disease—even if he has renounced the world—is considered inferior. A wise man, with a serene heart and truthful speech, should avoid such a person.

Likewise, having examined him, the teacher should protect him; for the examination of the characteristics of both teacher and disciple is essential for the sake of that knowledge, provided one seeks a teacher who possesses it. For the Śruti says: "One should approach [the teacher] with palms joined, with a tranquil mind, endowed with self-restraint and peace. Furthermore, the teacher should be one whose defects are stilled, who is entirely free from attachment, eternally devoted to the practice of the knowledge of Brahman.

A renunciant (*yati*) engaged in the cultivation of the "I-am-ness" (*vohaṃbhāvanā*) has reverence for ashes and purity; elsewhere... [there is] the lineage, consciousness, the examination of the disciple... (l. 6). O best of Brahmins, it is certain that the teacher’s... conduct, the thorough knowledge of the *ṛṣi*, *gotra*, and lineage, as well as the thorough knowledge of the limits of the duties regarding marriage and so forth, are likewise conducive to knowledge. (l. 7). And it is said: "One should not appoint as a teacher one who is a village-dweller (*grāmabhikṣu*), wrathful, or deceitful; for by the portion of iron, he consumes the food [of others], and so forth. Therefore, according to what has been stated... (l. 8b, l. 1).

One should obtain [initiation] from the mouth of a guru, through the signs of detachment, and so forth. If a wise person, in the absence of a guru as previously described, should undertake renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) together with its constituent parts in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti—provided that, in the absence of a teacher possessing the aforementioned characteristics, he himself performs it in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the teacher who bestows the water of knowledge to those blinded by the scriptures, and which is endowed with the characteristics such as the taking up of the staff and other requirements—if, due to the unavailability of a Kālī-kha[nda]-guru, [he does so] in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

One should take up renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and the *arṇava* [mantra], and [attain] the infinite... for all of them... Mahādeva... [says]: "There is no failure in the accomplishment of the eight foremost mantras. And thus, according to the *Prapañcasāra*, there is this unprecedented injunction: the mantra should be consecrated one hundred and eight times... Not only is he not excluded from the objects of the world when detached, but furthermore, during the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*), in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), having performed his daily rites (*āhnika*) at a great river in the city of Śikāya—

Having firmly resolved upon the purpose of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), one should perform the *kāṣāya* [donning of the ochre robe]. It is also remembered that for the deities, there is the consecration of tanks and the like, the tying of the sacred grass girdle (*mauñjībandhana*), the formal adoption of an ascetic order (*āśrama-svīkṛta*), the ritual release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*), and the departure [from worldly life]. Having performed the rites for the sake of specific desires (*kāmya-karma*) and having abandoned all impurity, one should avoid the following: the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth days of the lunar fortnight; likewise, [the new moon and full moon days]. Thus. (Note: The text provided contains several archaic or corrupted forms, such as *kraścaṃ* for *kāṣāyaṃ*, *smaryate* for *smarthyate*, and *vṛtārābhasamā...* which appears to be a corruption of *vṛttārādhana-samāptau*. The translation reflects the most probable intended meaning based on standard Sanskrit conventions.)

At auspicious times (*puṇyakāla*), one should perform four *kṛcchra* [penances] for the sake of attaining [the goal]. Yājñavalkya stated that procedure as follows: "By eating once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only every second meal, and by fasting—this is declared to be a *pādakṛcchra*. When performed in this manner, it is called a *prājāpatya*, which is threefold [in merit]. For one unable to perform the *prājāpatya*, [one may instead] give cows for purification, or half of that, or even a quarter."

Now, it is argued that a thousand *trihoma* oblations with *gāyatrī* verses is improper. For the *Sannyāsa Upaniṣad* states: "One desiring renunciation (*sannyāsa*) who is not yet an ascetic (*āśramin*) should perform four *kṛcchra* penances; having performed one *kṛcchra*, an ascetic is fit to renounce. It then describes an expiation for a specific occasion: "He who, having made a firm resolve for renunciation, subsequently acts contrary to it, should perform a *māṣa-kṛcchra* and is then fit to renounce again. Furthermore, it declares the transgression incurred in failing to conduct both examinations:

Those three who cause a renunciant to fall from his state of renunciation are known as sinners; therefore, one should [punish them] according to their merit. Now, having first performed the eight Śrāddha rites, one should likewise satisfy the gods and the ancestral manes (deva-pitṛs).

...other wise men consider only this procedure here. The practitioner, having abstained from leafy vegetables produced by passion for meat and the like, and after performing the *kṛcchra* penance, should—after the *vaiśvadeva* rite at midday—satisfy the deities intended for the *śrāddha* with water for the ancestors (*akṣatodaka*) and perform the *śrāddha* according to the rules of formal resolve (*saṃkalpa-vidhi*). For those following the *Dhāyyāyaṇa* and *Āśvalāyana* Sūtras, [the procedure] beginning with the mantra "yan me mātā... and so forth, up to the point of the offering of food, is as follows...

Regarding the statement "the offering to the ancestors" (*vāpārṣaṇam*), they desire [to know] that; therefore, he now describes the nature of the *śrāddha* for the gods: One should satisfy Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the gods who are transformations of Brahman; likewise the Kṣatriya sages (*kṣatrarṣi*), the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and Sanaka and the others; as well as the collection of organs such as the eyes, the group of the eight *patra*s, the group of the *mātra*s, and the group of the *ātman*s—these one should satisfy in the *śrāddha* prior to [the rite for the ancestors].

And likewise, in the *Parivrājaka-śruti*, it is said: "Now, one should perform eight *śrāddhas* for the ancestors, namely: Devas, Sages, Divine Beings, Humans, Pitṛs, and the Self. This will now be explained here in detail. First, the Viśvedevas known as Satya and Vasu; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara in the *Daiva* [śrāddha]; the celestial sages (*devarṣi*), brahminical sages (*brahmarṣi*), and royal sages (*kṣatrarṣi*) in the *Ārṣa*; the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas in the *Divya*; and Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, and [Sanātana] in the *Mānuṣa*.

The five oblations are earth and so forth; the fourfold group of oblations consists of the sense organs, such as the eye, and the material elements derived from them. [The ancestors are] the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather; [the female ancestors are] the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother.

In the *mahyomātra-śrāddha*, the Ātman, Antarātman, and Paramātman are to be worshipped in the *ātma-śrāddha*. Thus, at the outset, one should perform the *śrāddha* with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), water, incense, and the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as the vessel. He states the procedure for the *śrāddha*: "Thinking, 'I shall accept the renunciation known as the Parahaṃsa, which brings about auspiciousness by means of liberation from ignorance and leads to the attainment of Śiva, for the sake of quelling the fever of worldly existence through the path of the planets,' he should proceed."

Then, having uttered, "I shall perform the *śrāddha* for the *Aṅga-mṛṣṭas*," one should perform the *daiva-śrāddha* for the Viśvedevas, who are of the nature of Satyavasu, the Ānandīmukhas, and the deceased ancestors. This is to be done with water containing sesame seeds (*tilodaka*), excluding the *apasavya* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder) and other such rites, and beginning instead with the scattering of unbroken rice (*akṣata*) and water. The following are to be excluded: the invocation (*āvāhana*), the offering of the *arghya*, and likewise the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire). Furthermore, the touching of the thumb (*prāṇana*) is performed with the thumb alone, according to the mantra for the thumb.

Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) there, having offered oblations (*homa*) and worshipped with the *sanādi* [mantras], and having recited the mantra beginning with "He who is the consumer of the sacrificial offerings (*viśivabhuk*), the thumb-sized person residing within the thumb," and having uttered the words of Śiva—"Śiva is the enjoyer, Śiva is this entire world"—one should perform the offering to Śiva (*śivārpaṇa*). During the meal, one should be absorbed in the contemplation of Śiva while reciting the hymns (*sūktas*). At the end of the meal, one should offer the *piṇḍas*, saying "Svāhā" and "Namaḥ" in due order.

Having caused those who have recited the *Sūktāni*, the *Āvasathyopaniṣad*, and so forth, to eat until they are satisfied, one should offer three *piṇḍas* each, pronouncing the names of the respective groups at the end of each.

The meaning is that one should give them in order—saying "O Brahman, this *piṇḍa* is for you, svāhā," and "O Viṣṇu, [this is] for you"—upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, accompanied by unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and water, while reciting the *daivatyā* mantra. On the following day, having set aside half of the remnants of the ritual for the seventh [generation], and having bathed again and become pure, one should distribute [the remainder] entirely to all, except for one's own immediate needs. One may keep for oneself whatever is required for immediate use.

On the day before [the initiation], having established the site for success, measuring it with a span of eight finger-breadths, and having performed the sowing of seeds, bathing, the putting on of the sacred thread (*upavīta*), and the fivefold purification (*pañcagavya*), the practitioner should, at that time, perform the rites for his own teacher. Having given wealth as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brāhmaṇa, he should give [the remainder] to someone who has arrived, or [dispose of it] in a temple, a village, a river, a cow-pen, or a forest. Joining his palms in reverence (*brahmāñjali*) and uttering this mantra: [The mantra follows: *eme...* (as per the source).

[One should recite] the *brahmendrasūryasomasatya-jñāna-satya-satāraka* [mantra]. In a pure place such as a temple, having placed the right knee on the ground, with the left hand holding food and two *darbha* blades (*kurca*) placed upon it, and covering it with the right hand, one should mutter the seven mantras known as *brahmaṇe namaḥ*, and likewise those for Indra, Sūrya, Soma, Atman, Jñāna, Satya, and Satāraka. Having established the fire in the evening, one should perform the *saṃhṛti* (withdrawal) rite by means of the *dhākhena* [formula].

Having offered an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *ātman* and other mantras, he should himself drink the parched grain (*saktu*). Having established the fire according to his own Vedic branch (*śākhā*), and having recited the beginning and end of that branch starting with the hymn "agnim īle" and the *vyāhṛtis*, or alternatively, having offered after the establishment of the Brahman with the mantra "oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā," and having completed the subsequent mantra, he should first consume three handfuls of parched grain with the words "ātmane namaḥ" and "paramātmane namaḥ," as well as milk and drops of clarified butter. Thereafter follows the method for the withdrawal of the Vedic branches (*śākhopasaṃharaṇa*).

Oṃ bhūr, I cause Sāvitrī to enter; we meditate upon that adorable splendor of the Sun; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I cause Sāvitrī to enter; we meditate upon the divine light; Oṃ suvaḥ, I cause Sāvitrī to enter; may she impel our intellects. Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I cause Sāvitrī to enter; we meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the Sun, the divine light, which impels our intellects. Then, having applied [the unguent], he stands upon a black antelope skin facing north.

One should remain awake at night and listen to the *Ātmabodha-purāṇas*. Having established the implements—the saffron robe (*kāṣāya*), water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), staff (*daṇḍa*), and so forth—either to the north of the fire or there itself, one should stand and listen to the *Svarūpabheda-naya-purāṇa*. Then, at dawn, having performed the entire rite beginning with the bath according to one's own rule, one should offer oblations of ghee twenty times with the *Virajā-huti* mantra. After performing the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other rites, and having smelled the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), one should worship the fire and smell it with the mantra, "O Agni, go... (*yāte agne*).

Then, after the morning oblations beginning with the bath and so forth, having performed the *kālahoma*, the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, and other rites, and having completed the *virajā-mantra* and the *prāṇāhuti-mantra* for the sacrificial porridges (*caru*) and clarified butter (*ājya*) up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the *brahmācārya*. Thus says the Śruti: "Then, having sipped water (*ācamya*), having given a garment along with a sacrificial fee and a vessel for his own use, and having completed [the rite], [this is] the *brahmodvāpana*."

In the passage beginning with *upasthāya* (l. 8), it is understood that there is a request to Agni accompanied by the recitation of the *Viśvāmitra-ṛṣi* verses. The Blessed One (l. 11b, l. 1) states: "Until marriage, one should perform this very rite of attendance [to the fire] until death; there is neither the placing nor the removal [of the fire]"—by virtue of this statement, the *laukika-agni* (worldly fire) is maintained for the *brahmacārins* and *snātakas*. For those of the [three] castes, there is the offering of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*); for the *snātaka*, that [duty] remains constant. The *aupāsana-agni* belongs to the householder; likewise for those who have passed through [the stages]. For all, the *homa* is distinguished in some cases by the sequential renunciation (*krama-saṃnyāsa*).

Although there is no difference between the *brahmacārī* and the *snātaka* in terms of possessing the single fire (*ekāgni*), for the *brahmacārī* the fire is that which he kindles at the time of marriage (*samāvartana*), whereas for the *snātaka* who is a householder, it is the *aupāsana* fire. For those who are widowers (*vidhura*), there is only the single fire; thus, for all of them, upon renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), their own respective fires alone remain. The meaning is that there is no oblation with the *virajā-mantra*. Having worshipped one's own fire according to the rule with the words "O you who are well-established," the re-depositing of the fire into oneself should take place with the mantra beginning with "This is the womb."

"May the ocean sprinkle me; may Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Agni sprinkle me with vigor and with strength. Having approached [the fire] with this mantra, "Of non-yoked womb... (AY 3.12.7), the Adhvaryu priest should cause the horse to smell the fire; thus it is prescribed.

...For in the Śruti it is said: "In that case, some say one should perform the Prājāpatya sacrifice, or one should not perform it; rather, one should perform only the Āgneyī [sacrifice]. For Agni is the vital breath (prāṇa); by this [Āgneyī sacrifice], he indeed makes the vital breath. Here, "vital breath" refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman). By means of this Āgneyī sacrifice, one attains the vital breath, which is the Supreme Self. Having thus explained the passage, he subsequently states the Viṣṭi sacrifice. (I.12a, l.1)

Having uttered the mantra of superimposition, "The womb is here," and having brought fire from the village, one should cause [the fire] to smell [the offering] as before; by the force of the Śruti, this refers to the case of one who is without sacred fires (*niragni*). Therefore, for those who maintain a single fire (*ekāgni*), those who maintain the three fires (*tretāgni*), celibate students (*brahmacārin*), and those who have completed their studies (*snātaka*), there is a specific rule regarding the superimposition of the fire with the mantra "The womb is here. Now, if fire is unavailable, their oblation (*homa*) should indeed take place with that mantra alone; just as it is in the case of the *agnaukaraṇa* rite, so it should be according to the Śruti.

If, for some reason, one cannot obtain the non-worldly fire (*alaukikāgni*), one should offer oblations into the water of a heated pot using the *daukta* mantra. Regarding this, the scripture states: "If one does not find fire, one should offer oblations into water; for water is indeed all the deities. Having offered with the mantra, 'I offer to all the deities, svāhā!', one should proceed with the rite of stability (*dhṛti*). Now, regarding the rule for the *praiṣa* (the call for action): having dissolved the *vyāhṛtis* into the limbs of the *praṇava*, [one becomes] a single entity. For one who is not obstructed, the *candas*, mantras, and the mind are directed toward the goal.

Having dissolved the three *vyāhṛtis* into the syllables of the *praṇava* (such as *a*, *u*, and *m*), one should pray: "I am Brahman, like the trunk of a tree," and "He who is the bull among the meters (*chandāsām ṛṣabhaḥ*). Having uttered the dismissal mantra beginning with "Oṃ bhūḥ, [this is] renounced" (*sannyastam*) and so forth in the prescribed order, and having offered water for fearlessness (*abhaya-jala*) and sipped it, one should untie the cord and cast the sacred thread (*upavīta*) into the water with the word "Brahman. Then, having cut the waist-string (*kaṭisūtra*), one should live wearing only gold.

"Oṃ bhūḥ, renounced by me; Oṃ bhuvaḥ... by me; Oṃ suvaḥ...; Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ... Thus one should recite [the syllables] slowly, moderately, rapidly, or even with great intensity. Then, one is liberated from the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds.

Having pledged with a smile to grant fearlessness to all beings, saying "Bhakta-svāhā," he should sip a handful of water, perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), and bind his topknot (*śikhā*) with the *praṇava* (OM), then release it. (L. 2) With the *tāra* (OM), he should release the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and wear it outside; then, entering within, he should say: "O you who are eternally present, the supreme purifier, bestow upon me at all times strength, knowledge, dispassion, intelligence, and the purity of the inner being. (L. 3) Having performed the binding according to the procedure prescribed in the Śruti, he should cast water with the *praṇava*, and having discarded the waist-thread and other ornaments, he should remain wearing only his natural form (*jātarūpadhara*).

"Based on the Vedic injunction, 'One should remain always as if a child,' one should proceed toward the northern direction like a newborn infant, indifferent to the distinctions between one's lineage, sacred thread, enemies, and so forth. Having performed the recitation of the *vidāraṇapraiṣa* mantra, being solely intent on meditation upon the single syllable Om (*praṇava*), one should say, 'Fearlessness to all beings; [I am] liberated, Svāhā! Having placed the *turyātītāvadhūta* doctrine in his mind, he spoke thus: "With arms raised, having abandoned everything, thinking 'I am Brahman,' one should wander like a god, wearing the appearance of a newborn."

Alternatively, having obtained the staff, the garment, the bowl, and the water-pot—these being permitted by the Teacher according to the degree of one’s own dispassion—one should adopt them. Or, in the absence of the aforementioned dispassion, one may acquire the requisites characterized by the specific distinctions taught by the mouth of the Guru, in accordance with the ripening of one’s own mind. For it is said that the former [set of requisites] is primary; however, if one is not a candidate for those, then, at the request of a householder, one may take up the staff and so forth as a means of protection for oneself and others.

Having received the instruction on the *praṇava* and the great sayings (*mahāvākya*) from the presence of the Guru, one should engage in the hearing of the Vedānta. Having abandoned the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), one should [wear] the loincloth, the staff, and so forth, upon one's own body.

If it is asked, "Who then is the primary recipient for the sake of performing service to the world?"—the answer is that, according to the Vedic revelation beginning with "neither a staff nor a loincloth," the intention refers specifically to one who has transcended the [previous] stages of life (*āśrama*). In this world, there exist great souls who possess both higher and lower knowledge and who bring auspiciousness to the world; having assumed the role of teachers toward wretched people, they engage themselves in order to demonstrate the tradition and to instruct in the Vedic dharma of the castes and stages of life.

Whatever belongs to those excellent teachers—whether chariots, elephants, horses, thrones, umbrellas, chowries, chests, messengers, soldiers, servants, or other such things that benefit the world, rather than being for the enjoyment of their own desires—that very thing must be dedicated to the gods and so forth. [Thinking], "Such is this vehicle for the sake of the world," one should experience the prostration at the feet of the Great Being.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that [the rule] 'only a pair of loincloths and a single staff are to be accepted'—by the statement that 'more than this is forbidden'—implies that there is a sin for accepting more, and thus how can there be the possession of vehicles, umbrellas, and so forth? [Reply: True. Just as for the *vividiṣā-saṃnyāsin*, there is a contraction of the dharma of total renunciation characterized by *saṃnyāsa* for the sake of liberation; likewise, for the sake of gradual liberation, [this applies] to those who have descended as kings of the Śiśava lineage among a multitude of subjects.

The prosperity of the lineage of gurus who hold the tradition of the knowledge of the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda’s feet—which serves as a means for the deliverance of many people—is ordained from day one; just as [the prosperity] of kings is not destroyed by hunting and the like, nor by Indra’s instruction regarding the creation of uneven creatures, nor by Hari’s slaughter of the sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu, nor by Rudra’s universal destruction. Furthermore, even sinful deeds become well-conducted through the intent for the sovereignty of the Lord; they are indeed purified, there is no doubt.

(1.2) "I am distinct from the assembly of the ignorant, such as Māna, Vidu, Goha, and others, like the sky; I am eternal and immovable like a mountain; I am devoid of limits like the ocean"—for one who possesses such certainty of their own nature, there exists a specific splendor (*tejo-viśeṣa*) by virtue of the principle that "it is known through direct perception. However, the grasping of objects such as sound and so forth, as well as the worlds, is indeed a mere seizing; but [the yogi] knows that these are merely other desirable things consisting of earth and so forth, joined with deer, elephants, garlands, women, and music, [all of which are] below. (1.4) He states the definition of the staff (*daṇḍa*):

The ascetic (yati) should carry a bamboo staff (daṇḍa) that is smooth, with white bark, of even thickness, reaching to the nose, and level with the head. It should be of a height from the feet to the top of the head, unblemished, gentle, without a crooked tip, made of auspicious bamboo, and should be taken up preceded by the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). With the mantra: "O friend, you are my protector; you are Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; grant me protection and ward off evil," he should grasp the staff, according to the Śruti.

The *nāgamudrā* is [formed] by means of a cloth-strip (*vastrakhaṇḍa*) and should be held upon the staff; likewise, the *paraśumudrā* [is applied] to the base, middle, and tip of the staff in succession. Here, the *paraśumudrā* is indeed desired by all. Furthermore, there is the *brahmamudrā*, the *yenmudrā*, the *nāgamudrā*, and the *śaṅkhamudrā*; these four exist through the distinction of wrapping and knotting, and they are to be understood according to the sequence of oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*). Thus, there are five mudrās in total. For this very reason, the Guru says: "The staff, adorned with the five mudrās, is Śiva himself."
In the Ekādaśarudrasaṃhitā, [the world] up to the end of the Jagajjīvana [is established] by means of the *kuṇḍaka* and the *praṇava*.

One should receive the *kaṣāya* robe and other items from the words of the Guru. O Mother, who are the life-force and the support of the life of the world, always address me as "Obeisance to all that is auspicious. With the *praṇava*, one should accept the *maṇḍala*, the staff, the loincloth, the upper garment, the meditation-band (*yogapaṭṭa*), and so forth; such is the Śruti. Thus, the yogin possessing these means should choose a teacher of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). One who knows the reality of the meaning of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) becomes the supreme Brahmin. This is clear. Now, regarding the subject of the sacred fires (*agnihotra*):

One who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should then perform the Āgneyī and the Tridhātavī iṣṭis according to the procedure of the Praṇītā-māsa; he should avoid everything else. Regarding the case of one who has maintained the sacred fires, the performance of the Āgneyī and Tridhātavī iṣṭis is carried out by means of the Praṇītā-māsa procedure at the time of the employment of the vessels: [the sacrificial portions] and the Anyāhārya pot...

Excluding the *varjam-bhūta* [portion], it is like the nature of the vessel and the water. At the placing of the potsherds (*kapāla-upadhāna*) with the formula "pleasing to such-and-such deity," there is a repetition of the mantras for the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth [potsherds]. For this is indeed the sacrifice; "O Agni, perform the four-fold invocation for me; sacrifice to Agni; this is for Agni. O God, may I be worthy of sacrifice through Agni; there is no *pārvaṇa-homa*.

Having offered the *nāriṣṭha* and *sviṣṭakṛt* oblations, and having become detached [from the ritual], he consumes the *prāśitra*. In the division into four parts (*caturdhākaraṇa*), having given his own mother’s share and all the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the sacrifice becomes manifest; [he performs] the *iṣṭi* concluding with "the sacrifice is the ladle" (*yajñaśaṃca*), excluding [the usual formula]. Having completed the sacrifice, he places the vessels made of precious metal (*taijasa*) into the *āhavanīya* fire.
